session.question: How FT's do they add their own personal interpretation to sustainability requirements when they fulfill their boundary-spanning role?
session.answer:
First-tier suppliers (FTs) do not mechanically relay sustainability requirements from the focal firm to second-tier suppliers (STs). Instead, when acting as boundary spanners, they engage in sensemaking and enactment, translating the requirements as they pass them upstream and often adding their own interpretation. This interpretation is shaped by downstream social capital, especially cognitive capital and relational capital with the focal firm. In practice, this means FTs may decide whether to treat a requirement as a minimum compliance issue or as an opportunity for improvement-oriented supplier development. (jia2021theboundaryspanningrole chunk 1)

The key mechanism is that FTs exercise discretion in how they understand, filter, and implement sustainability standards. Their personal judgment, influenced by the quality of their relationship with the focal firm and shared understanding of sustainability goals, affects how rigorously or constructively they apply the requirements to STs. As a result, sustainability demands are not transferred in a uniform way; they are locally interpreted and operationalized in upstream relationships. (jia2021theboundaryspanningrole chunk 1)

pqac-69c997d6: This paper examines how first-tier suppliers (FTs) act as boundary spanners between a focal firm and second-tier suppliers (STs) in sustainability-oriented supplier development. It finds that FTs do not simply pass on sustainability requirements unchanged: they may add their own personal interpretation when fulfilling their boundary-spanning role. This interpretation is shaped by downstream social capital, especially cognitive and relational capital with the focal firm, and can influence whether FT actions toward STs are compliance-oriented or improvement-oriented. The study highlights that FTs exercise discretion in sensemaking and enactment of sustainability standards, translating requirements as they move them upstream.
From Meng Jia, Mark Stevenson, and Linda C. Hendry. The boundary-spanning role of first-tier suppliers in sustainability-oriented supplier development initiatives. International Journal of Operations & Production Management, 2021. URL: https://doi.org/10.1108/ijopm-12-2020-0856, doi:10.1108/ijopm-12-2020-0856.

pqac-08888339: This paper is relevant because it shows that first-tier suppliers acting as boundary-spanners do not simply transmit sustainability requirements unchanged. In the apparel industry cases, FTs sometimes add their own personal interpretation when fulfilling their boundary-spanning role. The study distinguishes between compliance-oriented and improvement-oriented actions and finds that downstream cognitive and relational social capital influence how FTs interpret and act on sustainability demands in upstream relationships with second-tier suppliers. It suggests that sustainability requirements are often filtered through relationships and local judgments in practice, rather than being applied in a purely uniform or mechanical way.
From Meng Jia, Mark Stevenson, and Linda C. Hendry. The boundary-spanning role of first-tier suppliers in sustainability-oriented supplier development initiatives. International Journal of Operations & Production Management, 2021. URL: https://doi.org/10.1108/ijopm-12-2020-0856, doi:10.1108/ijopm-12-2020-0856.

pqac-af5c2013: The excerpt is about supply chain managers’ cognitive frames and their implications for sustainable supply chain management. It says the paper develops three ideal-type frames—unidimensional, hierarchical, and paradoxical—and argues that the frame a manager holds affects how sustainability-related decisions are made. It also notes that the study discusses antecedents explaining why a manager adopts a particular frame. However, the excerpt does not specifically discuss FT boundary spanners, nor does it provide direct evidence on sensemaking, discretion, translation, or enactment of sustainability standards/requirements.
From Lutz Preuss and Andrew Fearne. Cognitive frames held by supply chain managers: implications for the management of sustainability in supply chains. Supply Chain Management An International Journal, 2021. URL: https://doi.org/10.1108/scm-08-2020-0364, doi:10.1108/scm-08-2020-0364.

pqac-8005606c: The excerpt is about supply chain managers’ cognitive frames and how these affect sustainable supply chain management. It argues that managers’ interpretation of sustainability-related decisions matters and identifies three ideal types of frames: unidimensional, hierarchical, and paradoxical. The paper emphasizes the boundary-spanning role of supply chain managers and says understanding their cognitive processes is crucial for how firms address sustainability challenges. However, it does not discuss frontline employees specifically, nor does it provide direct evidence about practical interpretation of CSR, ESG, or environmental compliance requirements by employees or other boundary spanners.
From Lutz Preuss and Andrew Fearne. Cognitive frames held by supply chain managers: implications for the management of sustainability in supply chains. Supply Chain Management An International Journal, 2021. URL: https://doi.org/10.1108/scm-08-2020-0364, doi:10.1108/scm-08-2020-0364.

pqac-5e25defc: This paper is about green entrepreneurial orientation in manufacturing SMEs and how it affects triadic sustainable performance (economic, environmental, social). It argues that boundary-spanning search helps firms obtain external knowledge and resources to improve sustainability outcomes, and that it fully mediates the effect of green entrepreneurial orientation on economic, environmental, and social performance. Environmental dynamism strengthens links between boundary-spanning search and economic/environmental performance, but weakens the link to social performance. The paper treats boundary-spanning search as an external knowledge-seeking tool rather than a detailed account of frontline employees interpreting CSR/ESG/compliance requirements in daily practice.
From Ye Fang, Yi Yang, Haiyan Xia, Yixuan Shao, Xieguo Gu, and Jiaqiang Shen. Green entrepreneurial orientation, boundary-spanning search and enterprise sustainable performance: the moderating role of environmental dynamism. Frontiers in Psychology, 2022. URL: https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2022.978274, doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2022.978274.

session.formatted_answer:
Question: How FT's do they add their own personal interpretation to sustainability requirements when they fulfill their boundary-spanning role?

First-tier suppliers (FTs) do not mechanically relay sustainability requirements from the focal firm to second-tier suppliers (STs). Instead, when acting as boundary spanners, they engage in sensemaking and enactment, translating the requirements as they pass them upstream and often adding their own interpretation. This interpretation is shaped by downstream social capital, especially cognitive capital and relational capital with the focal firm. In practice, this means FTs may decide whether to treat a requirement as a minimum compliance issue or as an opportunity for improvement-oriented supplier development. (jia2021theboundaryspanningrole chunk 1)

The key mechanism is that FTs exercise discretion in how they understand, filter, and implement sustainability standards. Their personal judgment, influenced by the quality of their relationship with the focal firm and shared understanding of sustainability goals, affects how rigorously or constructively they apply the requirements to STs. As a result, sustainability demands are not transferred in a uniform way; they are locally interpreted and operationalized in upstream relationships. (jia2021theboundaryspanningrole chunk 1)
